title: Consistency as a Testable Property: Statistical Methods to Evaluate AI Agent Reliability
claim: Perturb a task instance, run the agent repeatedly, then score output and trajectory similarity with statistical tests to measure reliability.
layout: 2 rows: top left-to-right chain of 4 boxes, branching to 2 bottom boxes
description: A flow diagram in two tiers. The top row has four rounded lavender boxes joined by left-to-right arrows. The first is a benchmark instance x_0 (SWE-bench, Spider2-DBT, BFCL). Next is a perturbations box x_1..x_n, split into prompt-level (paraphrase, translation, noise) and task-level (decoy MCP, schema, output format). Then comes the agent (LLM + harness) with repeated runs. The last box holds the final outputs y_i and the trajectories τ_i = (a_1..a_T). From that last box, an elbow connector splits downward into two peach boxes. The left one, Output consistency, uses pairwise agreement k(y_i, y_j) and a U-statistic test. The right one, Trajectory consistency, covers composition drift (JSD), ordering drift (Levenshtein/GAK), a kernel MMD test and position-weighted diagnostics. Colors are muted and the text is dense, with math notation inline.
caption: Overview of the framework. A benchmark instance is perturbed in ways that should not change the correct answer, the agent is run on the base and perturbed inputs, then pairwise similarities between final outputs (output-level) and action sequences (trajectory-level) are aggregated into consistency statistics with associated hypothesis tests.
abstract: This paper establishes a rigorous measurement science for AI agent reliability, providing a foundational framework for quantifying consistency under semantically preserving perturbations. By leveraging $U$-statistics for output-level reliability and kernel-based metrics for trajectory-level stability, we offer a principled approach to evaluating agents across diverse operating conditions. Our proposal highlights the important distinction between the core capability and execution robustness of an agent, showing that minor task-level variations can induce complete strategy breakdowns despite the agent possessing the requisite knowledge for the task. We validate our framework through extensive experiments on three agentic benchmarks, demonstrating that trajectory-level consistency metrics provide far greater diagnostic sensitivity than traditional pass@1 rates. By providing the mathematical tools to isolate where and why agents deviate, we enable the identification and rectification of architectural concerns that hinder the deployment of agents in high-stakes, real-world environments.
